note: CC-Wire adversarial input corpus. ONE source of hostile bytes for every implementation, so Go and Rust cannot drift into disagreeing about what is refusable. Read by vaultchat-backend-go/internal/ccwire/fuzz_test.go (as fuzz seeds) and services/transport/rust/tests/adversarial.rs (as a table). Hand-written from the wire specification rather than dumped from either implementation, so neither can pass by agreeing with itself — the same rule codec.json and frame.json already follow.
howToUse: Every entry is hex, whitespace-insignificant. `accept` records whether a CONFORMING decoder may return a value: false means the bytes are unrepresentable and must be refused. It is NOT an assertion about which error. Liveness — the decoder returns rather than panicking, hanging, or allocating a declared-but-absent length — is asserted for every entry regardless of `accept`.

cases.name: empty
cases.why: No frame is zero bytes. The degenerate input every parser sees first.

cases.name: single zero byte
cases.why: Field number 0 is illegal in protobuf, and one byte cannot carry a frame.

cases.name: single high byte
cases.why: A lone continuation byte: a varint that never terminates.

cases.name: tag without value
cases.why: Varint tag present, payload truncated. The classic off-by-one read.

cases.name: varint truncated mid-continuation
cases.why: Continuation bit set on the final byte — the decoder must not read past the buffer looking for the rest.

cases.name: length-delimited with no payload
cases.why: Declares 127 bytes, supplies none. A declared length is a claim, never a capacity.

cases.name: malformed length
cases.why: The length varint is itself unterminated.

cases.name: overlong varint beyond 64 bits
cases.hex: 08 ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff
cases.why: Ten continuation bytes cannot fit a u64. Must be refused, not silently wrapped.

cases.name: field number zero
cases.why: Field 0 is reserved and can never appear on the wire.

cases.name: reserved wire type 6
cases.why: Wire types 6 and 7 do not exist; a decoder that guesses is a decoder that can be steered.

cases.name: declared length far beyond max_frame_bytes
cases.why: A ~4 GiB declaration inside six bytes. THE remote-OOM case: it must be refused ON THE DECLARATION, before any allocation.

cases.name: traffic_class UNSPECIFIED
cases.why: TRAFFIC_CLASS_UNSPECIFIED is never valid on the wire. A decoder that treats 0 as a default rather than a refusal lets a frame arrive with no scheduling class.

cases.name: seq = 0 with traffic_class CONTROL
cases.why: Lower boundary of the sequence space, in an otherwise minimal valid frame. traffic_class is REQUIRED — a frame without it is refused, which is what makes the bare-seq form below unrepresentable.

cases.name: seq = 2^53 (JavaScript safe-integer edge)
cases.why: seq travels as JS_STRING precisely so JavaScript cannot truncate past 2^53. This is the value that would prove it wrong.

cases.name: seq = 2^63 (sign-bit boundary)
cases.why: An implementation treating seq as int64 turns this negative.

cases.name: seq = u64 max
cases.hex: 10 01 20 ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff ff 01
cases.why: Upper boundary. Must not wrap to zero and restart the sequence space.

cases.name: seq without traffic_class
cases.why: A sequence number with no traffic class. Found by the Go/Rust parity check on its first run: the original fixture asserted these were acceptable and the decoder correctly refused them. Kept as a case because the fixture was wrong, not the parser.
